title: 2026-03-05 Redwood discovery - model selection (Nereid Analytics)
summary: Initial model-selection discovery with Nereid Analytics. Customer is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted and dedicated usage: low-latency chat for customer support (short context), and long-context summarization + retrieval for legal transcripts (100k+ tokens). Key constraints: strong data residency and SOC2 requirements, multilingual support (EN/ES/FR/DE + occasional Japanese), and tool-calling for internal knowledge-base wiring. Agreed to run benchmarks and share pricing + security docs.
next_steps: Samir to send tiered pricing + latency vs cost spreadsheet by 2026-03-09
Lena to propose benchmark test plan (latency & long-context gen) and provide test harness by 2026-03-12
Priya to review and confirm required compliance artifacts (SOC2, KMS integration) by 2026-03-10
Schedule technical deep-dive with infra team (private deployment scoping) week of 2026-03-16
action_items: Samir Patel: Send tiered pricing + latency/cost spreadsheet; due: 2026-03-09
Lena Ortiz: Share benchmark harness + sample prompt sets for multilingual + long-context; due: 2026-03-12
Priya Kapoor: Compile compliance questions and required attestations, upload to shared drive; due: 2026-03-10
transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-03-05
- Time: 16:00 PT
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Maya (CTO, Nereid), Diego (ML Eng), Priya (Security)

Summary (auto): quick discovery covering model families, context-length needs, multilingual, and hosting options. Some transcription errors present.

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Samir with Redwood, and with me is lena our solutions engineer. happy to kick off, maya, do you want to give a quick intro to the team and priorities?

[00:12] Maya: yeah hi all, maya here, we're nereid analytics, we do automated document understanding for enterprise legal and customer support use cases. diego is our ML engineer who runs inference pipelines and priya is our security lead. main reason for call is selecting models + hosting — we have two big flows: real-time support (low latency, short context) and massive document summarization + retrieval (very long context).

[00:30] Diego: and just to add, the long-context stuff can be 50k to 120k tokens depending on the doc batch. we also need spanish and french first-class support, occasional japanese.

[00:42] Lena: thanks, got it. that's a pretty wide spectrum. quick questions on traffic — what RPS are you seeing for the realtime support flow?

[00:50] Maya: peak around 60 rps, but average is 10-15, and we plan to grow. latency target is sub-250ms 95th for the support chat responses. for long-context it's batch-oriented so latency is less strict, but total cost per doc is a concern.

[01:15] Samir: makes sense. thinking about hosted vs dedicated vs private: hosted is easiest to get going, dedicated helps with predictable throughput and cost, and private/vpc/on-prem is for when you need strict networking and key control. Can you tell us about your compliance needs?

[01:30] Priya: SOC2 is a must, we also need audit logs for model inference, ability to use our KMS, and VPC peering — we prefer the private control plane option if the plan and cost make sense. also data residency in eu for some customers.

[01:45] Samir: good notes. Redwood has SOC2, support for customer-managed KMS, and VPC/private deployment options. i will send the compliance pack after.

[02:00] Diego: on the model side — we're looking at open models to avoid API lock-in and cost surprises. wondering about tradeoffs between say, Llama-family variants, Mistral-like models, and heavier models (we've prototyped with open-llama and openweights).

[02:20] Lena: yeah, so high level: smaller open models are cheaper but may struggle with complex instruction-following and multilingual edge cases. larger families (we run mistral and llama-2 style bigs) give better multilingual and reasoning. Redwood maintains a catalog of verified open models and also offers quantized/dedicated variants that can hit better throughput. note: transcription may hear "Llama two" as "lama two" sometimes.

[02:45] Maya: we've also been testing Anthropic and OpenAI in parallel, primarily for quality comparisons on legal prompts. cost is a big deciding factor though.

[03:00] Samir: totally. one lever is route — you can use a higher-quality bigger model for a small % of calls (canary/cost-balance) and serve the bulk on cheaper variants. batching and prefix-caching for repeated doc sections can drop token costs for long-context tasks.

[03:25] Diego: about tool-calling — we need to call internal knowledge-base APIs and do structured outputs (entities + citations). does redwood support function-calling / tool-calls across open models?

[03:40] Lena: yes, we provide structured output and function-calling primitives in the API. for some older open models we add a small guardrail layer in the runtime to stabilize output schema. there can be model-specific differences in how reliable the function-calling is, so that's something we'll test in the bench.

[04:05] Priya: for tool-calling we need to ensure the requests to our KB never log plaintext results to third-party services and that the KV cache is controlled. is that handled in private deployments?

[04:20] Lena: in private/vpc mode the control plane is customer-managed; we can disable or encrypt caches and ensure logs are forwarded to your SIEM. we also support customer KMS so plaintext never leaves under our control.

[04:45] Maya: good. for long-context, do you offer native 100k token windows or do we stitch windows with retrieval?

[04:58] Samir: two approaches: some model variants support very long context natively (we've onboarded models with >64k windows and experimented with 100k+ via chunking + KV cache). for very large docs most customers combine retrieval + summarization to limit the active context. we should benchmark both patterns for your dataset.

[05:25] Diego: the tricky part is preserving citation offsets and exact quoting from original doc for legal use. aggressive summarization can lose provenance. any thoughts?

[05:38] Lena: absolutely — for legal provenance we recommend retrieval with exact-text anchoring and then model-assisted citation generation. some of the open models are better at verbatim quoting; we'll include eval prompts that check for provenance.

[06:00] Maya: what's the suggested path for our timeline — we're aiming to pick a vendor and start PoC in 6 weeks for initial support flow, then expand to a dedicated/prod pilot for long-context in Q3.

[06:15] Samir: sounds feasible. immediate step is a short PoC with hosted or dedicated dev capacity depending on your security sign-off. since you prefer private for residency, we can run a hosted PoC with data residency set to EU region for the support flow while we scope the private deployment.

[06:35] Priya: we would prefer to avoid sending sensitive legal transcripts to hosted endpoints if possible. can the PoC run in private dev environment?

[06:45] Lena: yes we can provision a dedicated/private dev cluster for the PoC but that adds setup time — usually 2-3 weeks for the private control plane setup, versus immediate hosted. tradeoff between time-to-eval and security.

[07:05] Diego: bench details — we'd want latency numbers for 8k and 32k contexts for different models, plus throughput for your dedicated pools. also per-token cost estimates for quantized vs fp16 variants.

[07:20] Samir: noted. lena will put together a bench plan. we'll include models: small Llama-like 7b quantized, mid-size 34-70b mistral-style, and a large 70-180b family we have verified. we'll include streaming and function-calling checks and multilingual prompts.

[07:45] Maya: on multilingual — our Spanish and French traffic is significant, japanese occasional. are there measured benchmarks for non-English? some models drop off.

[07:58] Lena: good point — multilingual quality varies a lot. we'll run evals using your sample prompt sets. we also keep internal metrics showing relative performance per language for each model family, but those are approximate.

[08:15] Priya: security checklist: SOC2 report, data flow diagram, KMS key lifecycle, audit logs, ability to disable caching, SSO/SAML for console. can you send those?

[08:28] Samir: yes, i'll attach the compliance pack and a redwood security one-pager. also include our runbook for private deployments.

[08:40] Diego: curious about cost: do you have ballpark numbers for dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted pay-as-you-go?

[08:50] Samir: yes — hosted is pay-as-you-go (higher per-token), dedicated is a committed capacity model that gives lower per-token pricing and predictable throughput. we'll send a tiered pricing sheet with examples for your expected traffic.

[09:05] Maya: any known pitfalls when moving from hosted PoC to dedicated/private prod?

[09:12] Lena: main items are network setup (VPC, peering), key management, and model pinning/versioning so you don't see surprises on regressions. also planning for rollout with canaries and automatic fallback in case a dedicated cluster can't handle burst traffic.

[09:35] Diego: about function-calling reliability — is it model-agnostic in your runtime or does the reliability depend heavily on model?

[09:45] Lena: we add runtime adapters that normalize outputs and also run schema enforcement pre- and post-generation. that buys consistency but isn't magic — better models still produce more reliable structured output. we'll surface failure rates in the bench results.

[10:05] Samir: any blockers from your side for the PoC?

[10:08] Maya: need the compliance docs for our security review, and pricing to share with finance. diego needs the bench harness to plug into his infra.

[10:18] Samir: ok action items and owners we'll capture.

[10:22] Priya: quick question — do you support customer-managed hardware (on-prem box) or only VPC/on-prem package?

[10:30] Lena: we support VPC-hosted private control plane and a packaged on-prem offering for air-gapped cases, but fully customer-run hardware with no Redwood components is more of an advanced enterprise option — we can discuss with the infra team in the deeper scoping call.

[10:50] Diego: for the bench, would you be able to run tests against our staging dataset or should we run locally?

[10:58] Lena: both options are possible: you can provide anonymized samples for us to run in our dev clusters (with EU region + private KMS if needed), or we give you the harness and scripts to run locally against a dedicated cluster. we'll propose both in the bench plan.

[11:20] Maya: that works. can you also include a short list of recommended models by use-case (support vs legal summarization) — we saw mention of quantized 7b for support and 70b+ for legal, want to confirm.

[11:35] Samir: yes recommended mapping: 7-13b quantized for high-throughput low-latency support (but may need chaining for complex instructions), 34-70b for multilingual and stronger reasoning, and 70b+ or specialized long-context variants for legal summarization. we'll produce a short doc with the recommendations and expected cost/latency ranges.

[12:00] Priya: last thing, do you have any bench results comparing private dedicated GPU pools vs hosted for latency consistency?

[12:12] Lena: we have internal dashboards and some public benchmarks; we'll attach a sample tracing/latency screenshot and include guidance on autoscaling policies for dedicated pools to hit your 95th percentile SLOs.

[12:32] Samir: great. recap next steps: i'll send pricing + security pack, lena will send bench plan and harness, priya will circulate compliance questions, and we'll schedule the technical deep-dive for private scoping. any objections?

[12:48] Maya: none, looks good. thanks everyone.

[12:52] Samir: thanks — i'll follow up with calendar invite and docs.

(Transcript ends — timestamps approximate; some speaker labels may be imperfect.)
